The simplest way is a bag of words. Tip a document's words into a bag and shake it. You keep which words, and how many times, but not their order. Take three tiny documents. First, build a vocabulary: every distinct word, sorted. Here, that's nine. Then give each document a row, with one column per word. The first document has the word the twice, and cat, mat, on and sat once each. That's a document-term matrix. Every row has the same nine columns, so rows can be compared, added up, and handed to a classifier.

Sometimes all that matters is whether a word is there. This spam says free three times. The count vector keeps the three. The binary vector just marks a one, for present.

The bag has blind spots. Dog bites man and man bites dog make exactly the same bag. Real vocabularies run to tens of thousands of words, so almost every cell is zero. And great and excellent are just two unrelated columns. The bag knows nothing about meaning. One weakness has a neat fix, though: the most common words get the biggest counts, and say the least.

Here are three new documents: a cat on a mat, a dog in a park, a comet in the sky. By raw count, the word the leads every row, with two. But a column that's the same in every row can't tell the documents apart.

TF-IDF weighs each word by how telling it is. Start with inverse document frequency: divide the number of documents by how many contain the word, then take the natural log. The word the is in all three. Three over three is one, and the log of one is zero. Cat is in just one, so it gets the log of three, about one point one.
